subject.title: Maximus, to himself
subject.author: Charles Olson
subject.text:
I have had to learn the simplest things
last. Which made for difficulties.
Even at sea I was slow, to get the hand out, or to cross   
a wet deck.
               The sea was not, finally, my trade.
But even my trade, at it, I stood estranged
from that which was most familiar. Was delayed,
and not content with the man's argument
that such postponement   
is now the nature of
obedience,
               that we are all late
               in a slow time,
               that we grow up many
               And the single   
               is not easily
               known

It could be, though the sharpness (the achiote )   
I note in others,
makes more sense
than my own distances. The agilities

               they show daily
               who do the world's   
               businesses
               And who do nature's   
               as I have no sense   
               I have done either

I have made dialogues,
have discussed ancient texts,
have thrown what light I could, offered   
what pleasures
doceat allows
               
               But the known?
This, I have had to be given,
a life, love, and from one man   
the world.
               Tokens.
               But sitting here
               I look out as a wind   
               and water man, testing   
               And missing
               some proof

I know the quarters
of the weather, where it comes from,   
where it goes. But the stem of me,   
this I took from their welcome,
or their rejection, of me

               And my arrogance
               was neither diminished   
               nor increased,
               by the communication


2

It is undone business
I speak of, this morning,   
with the sea
stretching out
from my feet

title: Two Debts Olson Never Spells Out
standfirst: In 1953 Charles Olson published a poem that names no one, but two men are folded into it: the Gloucester poet he had just wounded in print, and the friend he would later name, permanently, on the dedication page of the epic this poem belongs to.

sections.heading: A Giant Who Calls Himself Slow
sections.body:
Charles Olson stood six foot eight, a physical fact people who met him tended to mention first. He had spent boyhood summers in Gloucester, Massachusetts from about the age of five, and by the time he wrote this poem he had already run part of a wartime information office, helped organize a presidential campaign, and [turned down two cabinet-level jobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Olson) in Washington to write poetry instead. None of that is what opens the poem.

> I have had to learn the simplest things
> last. Which made for difficulties.
> Even at sea I was slow, to get the hand out, or to cross
> a wet deck.
>                The sea was not, finally, my trade.

The confession only works because it's a downgrade. A man that size, who had never made his living anywhere near a boat, chooses the sea as the one place he'll admit to fumbling — and then, in the same breath, cancels even that: it was never his trade at all.

sections.heading: The Poet He Later Wounded in Print
sections.body:
In 1949 Olson read a poem in the magazine Imagi by Vincent Ferrini, a Massachusetts frame-maker who had worked shoe factories and General Electric before turning to poetry, and went to find him in Gloucester — [a visit Olson would later call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Ferrini), self-mockingly, a "fan call." The two grew close. It was Ferrini, not Olson, who is credited with bringing Olson and Robert Creeley together, and Olson's first Maximus poems were even addressed to Ferrini directly, as letters to Vincent.

Then he turned the sequence against him. A public-radio retrospective marking Ferrini's hundredth birthday describes Olson having ["cruelly enshrined Ferrini as the scapegoat poseur"](https://www.wbur.org/news/2013/06/20/poet-vincent-ferrini) in the Maximus Poems. One reader of the manuscripts, the poet Joe Wolff, has argued that "Maximus, to himself" was [sent to Ferrini afterward](https://worldatuningfork.com/xtra/charles-olson-a-student-guide-to-the-maximus-poem/), perhaps as a sideways apology — proof Olson could be exactly as hard on himself as he'd been on his friend. The line about the achiote, a seed whose sharp red dye Olson says he notices in others, reads differently once you know whose sharpness he might have meant.

sections.heading: The Man Who Gave Him "the World"
sections.body:
While Olson was writing this, he and Robert Creeley had already begun the correspondence that would run for the rest of Olson's life and [fill ten published volumes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Creeley) between 1980 and 1996. In an essay written that same period, [Projective Verse](https://paulenelson.com/organic-poetry/projective-verse/), Olson set down what became a founding slogan of the poetics the two men were building together:

> FORM IS NEVER MORE THAN AN EXTENSION OF CONTENT

— a principle Olson credited outright, writing that "so it got phrased by one, R. Creeley." Three years later, when Jonathan Williams, a former student of Olson's at Black Mountain College, [published the first volume](https://sotherans.co.uk/products/olson-charles-the-maximus-poems) of the Maximus Poems through his own Jargon Press, it was Creeley who supplied the introduction, printed separately and laid loose inside each copy. Near the end of "Maximus, to himself," among the few things Olson says he has actually been given rather than made — "a life, love, and from one man / the world" — [the scholar Peter Gizzi reads](https://writing.upenn.edu/epc/authors/gizzi/gizzi_on_creeley.html) that unnamed man as Creeley, the same friend Olson would later name, on the dedication page of the completed epic, [the Figure of Outward](https://www.abebooks.com/signed-first-edition/Maximus-Poems-Charles-Olson-Robert-Creeley/10256398836/bd).

sections.heading: A Shape Built to Hesitate
sections.body:
Olson's Projective Verse argued that a poem's line should be scored by the poet's breath, not by a metrical grid — that the page becomes a kind of notation, its gaps standing for pauses a reader's voice will actually take. "Maximus, to himself" is a demonstration piece for the theory. The lines about lateness don't just describe delay, they perform it, breaking and indenting mid-thought:

> that we are all late
>                in a slow time,
>                that we grow up many
>                And the single
>                is not easily
>                known

Five short lines to say what one sentence could manage. The stammer is the point: a poem about being slow to learn simple things is itself deliberately slow to arrive anywhere, its thought interrupted by white space the way the speaker admits his own attention keeps getting interrupted by other people.

sections.heading: An Itinerant Greek in a Mailman's Coat
sections.body:
The persona Olson wrote under for the rest of his life borrows its name from [a Greek rhetorician and philosopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximus_of_Tyre) of the late second century, Maximus of Tyre, whose forty-one surviving lectures argue through questions of ethics and the divine — and, more quietly, from Olson himself, whose own six-foot-eight frame made "Maximus" also just a fact about the man holding the pen. The town this modern Maximus addresses instead of Tyre is [Gloucester, which Olson called](https://www.capeanncosmos.com/gloucester-400-culture-folio/charles-olson-maximus-of-gloucester) both "a form of mind" and "a place to go fishing from," a place he'd summered in since childhood and where, as a young man, he worked summers delivering mail for the post office — following, without much comment, [the trade of his own father](https://poets.org/poet/charles-olson), a career postman back in Worcester.

By the time he wrote this poem Olson was already teaching at Black Mountain College, the experimental school in North Carolina, and within a few years he would become its last rector, closing it himself in 1957. An orator's mask, worn by a man who kept quitting the rooms where power actually sat.

sections.heading: Undone Business, Left Undone
sections.body:
The poem ends mid-thought, on a second numbered stanza that reads almost like a fresh start:

> It is undone business
> I speak of, this morning,
> with the sea
> stretching out
> from my feet

"Undone business" turned out to describe more than one morning's mood. Olson kept writing new Maximus poems for the rest of his life, still adding to the sequence at the time of his death from liver cancer on January 10, 1970 — seventeen years after "Maximus, to himself" was first printed. [The full sequence](https://www.neil.blog/articles/maximus-to-himself-by-charles-olson) wasn't gathered into one volume until 1983, thirteen years after he died, edited by the scholar George Butterick. [A recording of Olson reading](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/12/27/charles-olson-reads-maximus-to-himself-1963/) this particular poem aloud survives from 1963, a decade in. A poem that opens by admitting the speaker learns things last, and closes by calling his own life's project unfinished, turned out to be exactly right about the scale of what it was underestimating.
